method: The data rate of one spatial stream is the number of data subcarriers in the channel times the bits of the modulation times the coding rate, divided by the OFDM symbol time; the link rate multiplies that by the spatial streams. A 20 MHz 802.11n or 802.11ac channel carries 52 data subcarriers and a 40 MHz one 108; 802.11ac adds 234 at 80 MHz and 468 at 160 MHz, and 802.11ax uses 234, 468, 980 and 1960. The modulation carries 1 bit per subcarrier at BPSK, 2 at QPSK, 4 at 16-QAM, 6 at 64-QAM, 8 at 256-QAM and 10 at 1024-QAM, and the coding rate runs from 1/2 to 5/6 over MCS 0 to 11: 802.11n defines MCS 0 to 7 per stream with the stream count encoded in the index as 8 x (streams - 1) + MCS, 802.11ac MCS 0 to 9 with 256-QAM at 8 and 9, and 802.11ax adds MCS 10 and 11 at 1024-QAM. An 802.11n or 802.11ac symbol is 3.2 microseconds of data plus a 400 or 800 ns guard interval, so MCS 7 at 20 MHz gives 52 x 6 x 5/6 / 4 us = 65 Mbps and 72.2 Mbps with the short interval; an 802.11ax symbol is 12.8 microseconds plus 800, 1600 or 3200 ns, so 20 MHz MCS 11 gives 143.4, 135.4 and 121.9 Mbps and 80 MHz MCS 11 gives 600.5, 567.1 and 510.4 Mbps, the figures the vendor tables print. 802.11ac leaves a few index, width and stream combinations undefined because they would need a fractional number of coded bits per symbol: 20 MHz omits MCS 9 except with 3 or 6 streams, 80 MHz omits MCS 9 with 6 streams and also MCS 6 with 3 or 7 streams, and 160 MHz omits MCS 9 with 3 streams, so those are refused rather than given a rate the standard does not define. Goodput is the data rate times the MAC efficiency entered, the share of the air that carries payload once preambles, headers, acknowledgements, contention and retries are taken out; that efficiency is the user's own figure, between 10 and 95 percent, not a specification. Airtime is the stream demand divided by the goodput, and the streams figure is your airtime budget times the goodput divided by the demand, rounded down. Ranges are 10 to 95 percent MAC efficiency, 0.1 to 2000 Mbps of stream demand with up to two decimals and 10 to 100 percent airtime budget; an unknown standard, a width or guard interval the standard does not define, an MCS index above the standard's maximum, too many spatial streams, and every missing, non-numeric, three-decimal or out-of-range value are each refused with a message naming the field. The rate is the negotiated single-user rate: OFDMA resource units, MU-MIMO, aggregation, beamforming and vendor extensions are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: H3C - "01-Radio management configuration" (radio resources management configuration guide): the 802.11n MCS, 802.11ac VHT-MCS and 802.11ax HE-MCS data rate tables for 20, 40, 80 and 160 MHz with 400, 800 and 1600 ns guard intervals, including 65.0 Mbps at 20 MHz MCS 7, 433.3 Mbps at 80 MHz VHT-MCS 9 with one stream and 143.4, 286.8 and 600.5 Mbps at HE-MCS 11, plus the note that 802.11n raises a 20 MHz channel to 52 data subchannels

Siemens - "SCALANCE W700 802.11ax Performance data" reference manual, section 4 "Transmission speed": the 802.11n, 802.11ac and 802.11ax rate tables with 0.8, 1.6 and 3.2 microsecond guard intervals (143.4 / 135.4 / 121.9 Mbps at 20 MHz HE-MCS 11, 510.4 Mbps at 80 MHz with the 3.2 microsecond interval) and the dash that marks VHT-MCS 9 at 20 MHz with one or two streams as undefined
